metaData.originalTitle: "Epigrams in Programming" by Alan J. Perlis
metaData.title: Epigrams in Programming
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: A collection of 120 epigrams by Alan J. Perlis that distill profound, often paradoxical, truths about programming, software engineering, and the nature of computation.
metaData.summary: This is a classic collection of 120 aphorisms by Alan J. Perlis, the first Turing Award winner. The epigrams cover a vast range of topics from the nature of programming languages and data structures to software evolution, complexity, and the human aspects of computing. They are known for their wit, depth, and enduring relevance, offering insights that are as applicable today as they were in 1982. The collection touches on themes like abstraction, modularity, the trade-offs between simplicity and complexity, the pitfalls of optimization, and the often counterintuitive realities of building software systems.

mainPoints.point: Simplicity is a hard-won achievement, not a starting point.
mainPoints.explanation: Perlis states 'Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it,' suggesting that true simplicity in design comes from mastering and then stripping away complexity, not from avoiding it.

mainPoints.point: A programming language's true value lies in its ability to shape thought.
mainPoints.explanation: The epigram 'A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing' argues that the best languages offer new paradigms and mental models, not just syntactic convenience.

mainPoints.point: Software systems are inherently fragile and prone to decay.
mainPoints.explanation: Perlis observes 'In the long run every program becomes rococo - then rubble,' and 'Optimization hinders evolution,' highlighting that over-engineering and premature optimization lead to brittle, unmaintainable systems.

mainPoints.point: Great programming requires discipline and a focus on completeness over cleverness.
mainPoints.explanation: He argues that 'Programmers are not to be measured by their ingenuity and their logic but by the completeness of their case analysis,' prioritizing robustness and thoroughness over flashy solutions.

mainPoints.point: The human element is central to computing, often in paradoxical ways.
mainPoints.explanation: Epigrams like 'In man-machine symbiosis, it is man who must adjust' and 'Prolonged contact with the computer turns mathematicians into clerks and vice versa' explore the complex, often humbling, relationship between humans and their tools.

keyQuotes: A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing.
Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it.
Fools ignore complexity. Pragmatists suffer it. Some can avoid it. Geniuses remove it.
Programmers are not to be measured by their ingenuity and their logic but by the completeness of their case analysis.
In the long run every program becomes rococo - then rubble.

relatedArticles.title: How Claude Code works in large codebases: Best practices and where to start | Claude
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a comprehensive guide on deploying Claude Code in large codebases, emphasizing that success depends more on the 'harness' of configuration layers (CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins, LSP, MCP) than on the model alone, and outlines proven patterns for making codebases navigable, maintaining configurations, and assigning organizational ownership.

relatedArticles.title: Dario Amodei — Policy on the AI Exponential
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Dario Amodei argues that AI is advancing exponentially, creating a dangerous mismatch with slow-moving policy, and proposes concrete actions across regulation, economics, science, civil liberties, and geopolitics to meet the moment.

relatedArticles.title: The Claude Code Handbook: A Professional Introduction to Building with AI-Assisted Development
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A comprehensive professional guide to Claude Code, Anthropic's agentic AI developer tool, detailing its capabilities, model selection, and the transformative shift toward AI-assisted software engineering.

relatedArticles.title: Software Architecture Guide
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This page from Martin Fowler presents his perspective on software architecture, defining it as the important stuff in system design, and serves as a curated guide to his site's extensive resources on application and enterprise architecture.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineers detail a five-month experiment building a production software product with zero manually-written code, using Codex agents to achieve 10x velocity and redefining the engineer's role as system designer and feedback loop architect.

relatedArticles.title: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents， AutoResearch， and the Loopy Era of AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Andrej Karpathy explores the paradigm shift from manual programming to agent orchestration, the automation of AI research, and the profound implications for software engineering and education.

relatedArticles.title: Inside FAISS: Billion-Scale Similarity Search
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep, visual, and intuitive explanation of FAISS, covering the core ideas of IVF, Product Quantization, their combination in IVFPQ, and GPU acceleration, to enable billion-scale similarity search.

relatedArticles.title: Martin Fowler & Kent Beck: Frameworks for reinventing software， again and again
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Software legends Martin Fowler and Kent Beck discuss how AI redefines software engineering, emphasizing that core practices like TDD and modularity remain essential for human-AI collaboration.

relatedArticles.title: Xiaomi MiMo， Explore and Love
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Xiaomi MiMo and TileRT achieve 1000+ tokens/s inference on a 1-trillion-parameter model using commodity GPUs through extreme model-system codesign, including FP4 quantization and DFlash speculative decoding.

relatedArticles.title: Harness design for long-running application development
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores Anthropic's multi-agent harness design (Planner, Generator, Evaluator) for long-running autonomous coding, detailing how to overcome context anxiety and self-evaluation bias to build complex full-stack applications.
